title: Public IP Reachable but Domain Name Fails to Resolve
symptoms: Workstation users report they cannot open corporate intranet web portals or external websites by name (e.g. intranet.corp.local, github.com), but pinging public IP 8.8.8.8 succeeds.
environment: Enterprise Branch Office LAN (192.168.10.0/24), Cisco Catalyst Switch, DHCP Server on Gateway, Active Directory Internal DNS.
scenarioDescription: A user calls the IT help desk stating: 'The Internet is completely down for my computer, but my coworker can still access everything.' As the network administrator, you need to isolate the fault domain methodically starting from local host configuration up through DNS query resolution.

decisionPoints.title: Verify Local Workstation IP Configuration
decisionPoints.description: Begin by inspecting the client's current IPv4 configuration to establish a baseline of the client's IP, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Workstation Windows Command Prompt:
C:\> ipconfig /all

Ethernet adapter Ethernet0:
   Connection-specific DNS Suffix  . : corp.local
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.45(Preferred)
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.1
   DHCP Server . . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.10.250
   NetBIOS over Tcpip. . . . . . . . : Enabled

options.text: Immediately run 'ipconfig /release && ipconfig /renew' to re-request DHCP settings blindly.
options.feedback: Renewing DHCP without testing the existing gateway and DNS reachability destroys current state without telling you if the gateway or DNS server is reachable.

options.text: Ping the Default Gateway (192.168.10.1) and Public IP (8.8.8.8) to isolate Layer 1-3 network connectivity.
options.feedback: Optimal step: Testing the default gateway and a known public IP immediately separates local Layer 1/2/3 connectivity from application-layer DNS resolution issues.

options.text: Instruct the user to restart their computer to clear any transient network errors.
options.feedback: Blind reboots waste time, disrupt users, and provide zero root cause evidence.

decisionPoints.title: Test Layer 3 Gateway and Internet Reachability
decisionPoints.description: Execute ICMP echo probes to verify if the client can route traffic through the local default gateway and out to the Internet.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - ICMP Ping Connectivity Test:
C:\> ping -n 2 192.168.10.1
Pinging 192.168.10.1 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 192.168.10.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64
Reply from 192.168.10.1: bytes=32 time<1ms TTL=64
Ping statistics for 192.168.10.1:
    Packets: Sent = 2, Received = 2, Lost = 0 (0% loss)

C:\> ping -n 2 8.8.8.8
Pinging 8.8.8.8 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=14ms TTL=117
Reply from 8.8.8.8: bytes=32 time=13ms TTL=117
Ping statistics for 8.8.8.8:
    Packets: Sent = 2, Received = 2, Lost = 0 (0% loss)

options.text: Conclude that Internet routing is working properly, and test DNS resolution specifically using nslookup.
options.feedback: Optimal: Since both the default gateway and public IP 8.8.8.8 respond cleanly with low latency, Layer 1 through Layer 3 routing is healthy. The fault is isolated to DNS name resolution.

options.text: Replace the network patch cable connecting the workstation to the wall jack.
options.feedback: The cable is transmitting packets cleanly at Layer 1/2 with 0% packet loss and <1ms latency to the gateway. Replacing hardware is unwarranted.

options.text: Disable the Windows Defender Firewall on the workstation.
options.feedback: Disabling the local firewall weakens endpoint defense without addressing the fact that ICMP already succeeds bidirectionally.

decisionPoints.title: Probe DNS Name Resolution and Server Responsiveness
decisionPoints.description: Use nslookup to query both internal and external hostnames against the configured DNS server (192.168.10.250).
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - DNS Query Diagnostics:
C:\> nslookup intranet.corp.local
DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
*** Can't find intranet.corp.local: No answer

C:\> nslookup intranet.corp.local 192.168.10.250
DNS request timed out.
    timeout was 2 seconds.
*** Can't find intranet.corp.local: No response from server

C:\> ping -n 2 192.168.10.250
Pinging 192.168.10.250 with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 192.168.10.45: Destination host unreachable.
Reply from 192.168.10.45: Destination host unreachable.

options.text: Test DNS resolution against the known corporate Domain Controller at 192.168.10.10 and public DNS 8.8.8.8.
options.feedback: Optimal: By testing with an explicit DNS server IP (nslookup intranet.corp.local 192.168.10.10), you can confirm whether the real DNS server is operational and why 192.168.10.250 is unreachable.

options.text: Add intranet.corp.local and all external websites manually into C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts.
options.feedback: Editing the hosts file is an unmaintainable workaround that does not solve the root network problem and breaks dynamic DNS updates.

options.text: Delete the client's local DNS cache using 'ipconfig /flushdns' and retest.
options.feedback: Flushing local cache won't help when the configured DNS server IP (192.168.10.250) itself is completely unreachable.

decisionPoints.title: Cross-Verify DNS Server Availability and Scope Configuration
decisionPoints.description: Test queries against the primary corporate DNS server at 10.10.10.10 and inspect the local branch router's DHCP scope settings.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Explicit DNS Query & Router DHCP Scope:
C:\> nslookup intranet.corp.local 192.168.10.10
Server:  dc01.corp.local
Address:  192.168.10.10

Name:    intranet.corp.local
Address:  192.168.10.80

Router SSH Session (Router# show run | section dhcp):
ip dhcp pool BRANCH-OFFICE
   network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
   default-router 192.168.10.1
   dns-server 192.168.10.250 192.168.10.10
   lease 0 8

options.text: Identify that 192.168.10.250 is an invalid/decommissioned DNS server configured as primary in the DHCP pool, and proceed to final remediation.
options.feedback: Optimal deduction: The router's DHCP pool is handing out 192.168.10.250 as primary DNS. Because 192.168.10.250 is dead, queries time out before failing over or aborting. Updating the DHCP pool to 192.168.10.10 permanently resolves the issue.

options.text: Reboot the router to force all clients to renegotiate DHCP.
options.feedback: Rebooting the router will disrupt all active sessions across the branch office without fixing the misconfigured DNS IP in the running config.

finalDiagnosis.title: DHCP Scope Misconfigured with Decommissioned Primary DNS Server
finalDiagnosis.rootCause: The branch office DHCP scope on the default gateway (192.168.10.1) was distributing 192.168.10.250 as the primary DNS server. This server was decommissioned last week, resulting in 2-second query timeouts on all client DNS requests. The secondary DNS server (192.168.10.10) was fully functional but client lookups were failing or experiencing extreme latency.
finalDiagnosis.evidenceSummary:
1. Client had valid Layer 3 IP, subnet mask, and gateway.
2. ICMP ping to gateway (192.168.10.1) and public IP (8.8.8.8) had 0% packet loss and low latency.
3. nslookup directly to 192.168.10.250 timed out, and host was unreachable.
4. nslookup explicitly directed to 192.168.10.10 succeeded immediately.
5. Router DHCP pool showed 192.168.10.250 configured as the first DNS server.
finalDiagnosis.recommendedRemediation:
1. On the branch router: Remove 192.168.10.250 from the DHCP pool and set primary DNS to 192.168.10.10 with an active backup (e.g. 192.168.20.10).
2. Save router configuration with 'write memory'.
3. Instruct client workstations to run 'ipconfig /renew' to pull corrected DNS server attributes.
finalDiagnosis.verificationSteps:
1. Run 'ipconfig /all' on the client and verify DNS server shows 192.168.10.10.
2. Run 'nslookup intranet.corp.local' and verify immediate answer without timeouts.
3. Test browsing to corporate intranet portals and external web sites.
finalDiagnosis.preventionMeasures: Implement change management checks during infrastructure decommissioning to audit and update all DHCP scopes, static server configurations, and IPAM reservations prior to decommissioning legacy IP endpoints.

title: Domain User Sign-In Fails with No Logon Servers Available
symptoms: Users on newly booted Windows 11 enterprise workstations receive the error: 'There are currently no logon servers available to service the logon request' when attempting to sign in with Active Directory domain credentials.
environment: Active Directory Domain Services (corp.local), Windows Server 2022 Domain Controllers, Windows 11 Enterprise Hyper-V VM Clients.
scenarioDescription: A virtual desktop user cannot sign in on Monday morning. Cached credentials allow local login with limited privileges, but domain resources, mapped drives, and group policies fail to apply. You need to troubleshoot domain controller locator mechanics, network connectivity, and Kerberos dependencies.

decisionPoints.title: Check Workstation IP and Domain Network Profile
decisionPoints.description: Inspect network interface details to confirm the workstation has received valid IP parameters and can communicate with the local subnet.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - PowerShell Diagnostic Console:
PS C:\> Get-NetIPConfiguration

InterfaceAlias      : vEthernet (Default Switch)
IPv4Address         : 10.10.5.42
IPv4DefaultGateway  : 10.10.5.1
DNSServer           : 10.10.1.10
NetProfile.Name     : corp.local (DomainAuthenticated)

PS C:\> Test-Connection -TargetName 10.10.5.1 -Count 2 -Quiet
True
PS C:\> Test-Connection -TargetName 10.10.1.10 -Count 2 -Quiet
True

options.text: Unjoin the computer from the domain and rejoin it using local administrator credentials.
options.feedback: Unjoining and rejoining is a destructive, high-overhead step that invalidates user profiles, resets machine account passwords, and masks the underlying issue.

options.text: Query Active Directory DNS SRV records using nltest and nslookup to test Domain Controller discovery.
options.feedback: Optimal: nltest /dsgetdc checks the DC locator mechanism (DNS SRV record lookup and Netlogon ping over UDP 389) which is the core mechanism Windows uses to discover logon servers.

options.text: Restart the workstation 3 times to trigger automatic startup repair.
options.feedback: Startup repair fixes corrupted boot loaders, not domain network authentication failures.

decisionPoints.title: Examine Domain Controller Locator and DNS SRV Records
decisionPoints.description: Run nltest to verify if the Netlogon service can locate an operational Domain Controller in the corp.local domain.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - DC Locator Query:
PS C:\> nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local
           DC: \\DC01.corp.local
      Address: \\10.10.1.10
     Dom Guid: 3a2c5e71-9f44-48b2-b7e1-8899220011aa
     Dom Name: corp.local
  Forest Name: corp.local
 Dc Site Name: Default-First-Site-Name
Our Site Name: Default-First-Site-Name
        Flags: PDC GC DS LDAP KDC TIMESERV GTIMESERV WRITABLE DNS_DC DNS_DOMAIN DNS_FOREST CLOSE_SITE FULL_SECRET
The command completed successfully.

options.text: Verify Kerberos (TCP/UDP 88) and LDAP (TCP 389) port reachability to DC01 using Test-NetConnection.
options.feedback: Optimal: DC locator succeeded, so DNS SRV records and Netlogon ping are functional. The next logical step is verifying transport connectivity to the Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) on port 88.

options.text: Delete the computer account in Active Directory Users and Computers.
options.feedback: Deleting the Active Directory computer account severs the domain trust relationship completely, requiring offline domain rejoin.

decisionPoints.title: Audit Port Reachability and Kerberos Authentication Logs
decisionPoints.description: Test TCP port 88 connectivity to the DC and inspect the Windows System Event Log for Kerberos error events.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Port Reachability & Security Event Log:
PS C:\> Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 10.10.1.10 -Port 88
ComputerName     : 10.10.1.10
RemotePort       : 88
TcpTestSucceeded : True

PS C:\> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Kerberos-Key-Distribution-Center','Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service'; MaxEvents=2} | Format-List TimeCreated, Id, Message

TimeCreated : 9/15/2026 1:04:12 PM
Id          : 143
Message     : The Kerberos client received a KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW error from the server DC01$. The difference between the client time and server time is too large. A ticket cannot be issued until the clocks are synchronized.

PS C:\> w32tm /stripchart /computer:10.10.1.10 /samples:1 /dataonly
Tracking 10.10.1.10 [10.10.1.10:123].
13:05:00, +487.3241050s

options.text: Identify excessive Kerberos clock skew (+487 seconds, exceeding the 5-minute / 300-second Kerberos limit) caused by Hyper-V host time desynchronization, and proceed to remediation.
options.feedback: Optimal: Event ID 143 and w32tm output clearly prove the client clock is skewed by over 8 minutes. Active Directory Kerberos protocol strictly enforces a maximum 5-minute skew tolerance to defeat replay attacks.

options.text: Disable Kerberos authentication across the domain and force NTLM fallback via Group Policy.
options.feedback: Disabling Kerberos degrades domain security to vulnerable NTLM hashes, which is unacceptable and fails enterprise compliance baselines.

finalDiagnosis.title: Kerberos Authentication Blocked by Excessive System Clock Skew
finalDiagnosis.rootCause: The Windows 11 Hyper-V VM experienced clock drift during weekend host sleep/resume, causing its local time to deviate by +487 seconds (over 8 minutes) from the Domain Controller. Because Kerberos authentication protocol enforces a maximum clock skew tolerance of 300 seconds (5 minutes) to protect against ticket replay attacks, the KDC on DC01 rejected the AS-REQ with KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW, surfacing as 'No logon servers available'.
finalDiagnosis.evidenceSummary:
1. Workstation had active network connectivity and successful ping to gateway and DC.
2. DC Locator successfully resolved DC01.corp.local.
3. Test-NetConnection confirmed TCP port 88 (Kerberos) was listening and reachable.
4. System Event Log recorded Event ID 143: 'KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW: difference between client time and server time is too large'.
5. 'w32tm /stripchart' proved +487 seconds time delta between workstation and DC01.
finalDiagnosis.recommendedRemediation:
1. Resynchronize client clock against the domain hierarchy: Run 'w32tm /resync /force'.
2. If Windows Time service is stopped or misconfigured, re-register and start it: 'net stop w32time', 'w32tm /unregister', 'w32tm /register', 'net start w32time', 'w32tm /resync'.
3. Verify VM time synchronization integration service is enabled in Hyper-V VM settings.
finalDiagnosis.verificationSteps:
1. Run 'w32tm /query /status' to confirm source is DC01.corp.local and stratum is aligned.
2. Run 'klist purge' followed by 'klist' or attempt domain interactive logon.
3. Verify user signs in successfully and receives valid Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT).
finalDiagnosis.preventionMeasures: Configure Group Policy for Windows Time Service to ensure all domain members query the authoritative PDC Emulator, and configure Hyper-V host time synchronization integration components properly.

title: Web Application Service Fails to Start After Server Reboot
symptoms: Following a scheduled security patch and server reboot, the backend node service 'api-service.service' on an Ubuntu 24.04 LTS server fails to start with systemctl error code 1/FAILURE.
environment: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Server, systemd init system, Node.js backend application, Dedicated /mnt/storage partition in /etc/fstab.
scenarioDescription: The production operations team reports that an internal API service is down following automated kernel patch updates. The server is up and SSH is working, but the application daemon refuses to start. You need to inspect systemd service unit status, parse journalctl logs, and identify the root dependency failure.

decisionPoints.title: Inspect systemd Service Unit Status
decisionPoints.description: Query the service status using systemctl to inspect the exit code, PID status, and recent journal snippet.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - systemctl status output:
$ sudo systemctl status api-service.service
× api-service.service - Core Enterprise API Gateway
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/api-service.service; enabled; preset: enabled)
     Active: failed (Result: exit-code) since Mon 2026-09-15 08:22:11 UTC; 4min ago
    Process: 1042 ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /opt/api/server.js (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)
   Main PID: 1042 (code=exited, status=1/FAILURE)
        CPU: 124ms

Sep 15 08:22:11 srv-app01 systemd[1]: Starting api-service.service...
Sep 15 08:22:11 srv-app01 node[1042]: Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/mnt/storage/config/production.json'
Sep 15 08:22:11 srv-app01 systemd[1]: api-service.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Sep 15 08:22:11 srv-app01 systemd[1]: api-service.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.

options.text: Reinstall Node.js and re-run npm install across the whole application directory.
options.feedback: The error is ENOENT (file not found on path '/mnt/storage/config/production.json'), not a Node binary corruption or missing npm dependency.

options.text: Investigate filesystem mounts and verify if /mnt/storage is currently mounted using findmnt and df.
options.feedback: Optimal: The log indicates /mnt/storage/config/production.json is missing. In server operations, missing files on secondary mount points usually mean the filesystem failed to mount during boot.

options.text: Change ownership of /opt/api recursively to root:root with chmod 777.
options.feedback: Indiscriminate chmod 777 destroys filesystem security, violates principle of least privilege, and does not fix the missing file.

decisionPoints.title: Verify Filesystem Mounts and Disk Partition State
decisionPoints.description: Check whether /mnt/storage is mounted and review block devices using findmnt and lsblk.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Mount Table & Block Devices:
$ findmnt /mnt/storage
(returns empty exit code 1)

$ ls -la /mnt/storage
total 8
drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Sep 10 14:00 .
drwxr-xr-x 4 root root 4096 Sep 10 14:00 ..
(directory is completely empty)

$ lsblk -f
NAME   FSTYPE FSVER LABEL UUID                                 FSAVAIL FSUSE% MOUNTPOINTS
sda
├─sda1 ext4   1.0         4f8b9a10-22c1-4b72-9844-0192a83120ff   42.1G    38% /
sdb
└─sdb1 ext4   1.0   DATA  e51240c8-7f91-49b0-a332-6bb20145c110

options.text: Audit /etc/fstab to inspect the mount configuration for /mnt/storage against the actual UUID of /dev/sdb1.
options.feedback: Optimal: /dev/sdb1 exists with UUID 'e51240c8-7f91-49b0-a332-6bb20145c110' but is unmounted. Comparing /etc/fstab entries will reveal why it failed to mount at boot.

options.text: Format /dev/sdb1 using 'mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1' to create a clean filesystem.
options.feedback: Running mkfs formats the disk and destroys all production application data and configuration files permanently!

decisionPoints.title: Audit /etc/fstab Configuration and findmnt --verify
decisionPoints.description: Inspect /etc/fstab and test mount verification using findmnt --verify.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - /etc/fstab inspection:
$ cat /etc/fstab
# /etc/fstab: static file system information.
UUID=4f8b9a10-22c1-4b72-9844-0192a83120ff / ext4 errors=remount-ro 0 1
UUID=e51240c8-7f91-49b0-a332-6bb20145c119 /mnt/storage ext4 defaults 0 2

$ sudo findmnt --verify
/etc/fstab: parse error at line 3: [FAILED] UUID=e51240c8-7f91-49b0-a332-6bb20145c119: no such device found

options.text: Identify UUID typo in /etc/fstab (ending in 'c119' instead of 'c110'), correct the UUID, mount the disk, and restart api-service.
options.feedback: Optimal: The UUID in /etc/fstab had a single-digit typo ('c119' vs actual block device UUID 'c110'). Updating /etc/fstab and running 'sudo mount -a' will mount /mnt/storage and allow api-service to start.

options.text: Modify server.js code to disable production configuration file validation.
options.feedback: Bypassing configuration validation leaves the application running in an invalid unconfigured state without access to its persistent storage database.

finalDiagnosis.title: Typo in /etc/fstab UUID Prevented Secondary Disk Mount at Boot
finalDiagnosis.rootCause: During a prior disk maintenance window, an administrator updated /etc/fstab with a typographical error in the UUID for /mnt/storage ('...c119' instead of actual partition UUID '...c110'). Because the mount was not verified prior to reboot, systemd was unable to mount /mnt/storage at boot time. When api-service started, it crashed with ENOENT because its required configuration file '/mnt/storage/config/production.json' was absent on the unmounted mount point.
finalDiagnosis.evidenceSummary:
1. 'systemctl status api-service' logged exit status 1 due to missing '/mnt/storage/config/production.json'.
2. 'findmnt /mnt/storage' confirmed /mnt/storage was not mounted.
3. 'lsblk -f' revealed physical disk /dev/sdb1 had UUID 'e51240c8-7f91-49b0-a332-6bb20145c110'.
4. '/etc/fstab' showed erroneous UUID ending in '...c119'.
5. 'findmnt --verify' flagged the exact fstab parsing failure.
finalDiagnosis.recommendedRemediation:
1. Edit /etc/fstab with sudo and correct the UUID to 'UUID=e51240c8-7f91-49b0-a332-6bb20145c110'.
2. Add 'nofail' mount option if this volume is non-critical for OS boot: 'defaults,nofail'.
3. Run 'sudo mount -a' to mount all filesystems in fstab.
4. Run 'sudo systemctl start api-service.service' and verify status is active (running).
finalDiagnosis.verificationSteps:
1. Run 'findmnt /mnt/storage' and verify it shows ext4 on /dev/sdb1.
2. Run 'sudo findmnt --verify' and ensure 0 errors reported.
3. Run 'sudo systemctl status api-service' and confirm Active: active (running).
4. Send HTTP GET to API health endpoint: 'curl -I http://localhost:3000/health' (HTTP 200 OK).
finalDiagnosis.preventionMeasures: Mandate the use of 'sudo findmnt --verify' and 'sudo mount -a' before rebooting any server after modifying /etc/fstab, and utilize configuration management (Ansible) with UUID templating.

title: Virtual Machine Running but Internal Service Unreachable Across Network
symptoms: Other servers and load balancers on the subnet cannot connect to a backend analytics service on TCP port 8080. The hypervisor reports the VM is healthy and ping to the VM's IP address works.
environment: Enterprise VMware ESXi / Linux KVM Virtualized Infrastructure, Rocky Linux 9 Guest OS (IP 10.20.4.50), Backend Java Microservice.
scenarioDescription: A backend analytics VM was updated over the weekend. The virtualization team reports the VM is powered on with zero packet loss on ping, but client services receive 'Connection refused' whenever attempting to connect to port 8080. You need to isolate layered server networking and socket binding.

decisionPoints.title: Confirm Guest OS Status and Remote Reachability
decisionPoints.description: Establish an SSH session to the VM at 10.20.4.50 to verify guest OS health and test local connectivity.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - SSH & Local Connectivity Probe:
$ ping -c 2 10.20.4.50
64 bytes from 10.20.4.50: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.321 ms
64 bytes from 10.20.4.50: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.298 ms

$ ssh admin@10.20.4.50
Last login: Mon Sep 15 09:12:00 2026 from 10.20.4.100
[admin@srv-analytics ~]$ uptime
 09:15:02 up 14:32,  1 user,  load average: 0.12, 0.08, 0.05

options.text: Check the service status of analytics-backend using systemctl and examine listening ports with ss -tulpn.
options.feedback: Optimal: System uptime and SSH prove guest OS and network interfaces are running. Checking the service daemon and socket listener state immediately isolates whether the application is listening on the network.

options.text: Restart the virtual machine from the hypervisor console.
options.feedback: The VM is running normally with low load. Rebooting without investigating socket listeners will not fix configuration issues.

decisionPoints.title: Inspect Application Daemon and Active Socket Listeners
decisionPoints.description: Check if the process is active and determine which IP addresses and ports it has bound to.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Process Status & Socket Listeners:
[admin@srv-analytics ~]$ sudo systemctl status analytics-backend
● analytics-backend.service - Analytics Engine
   Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/analytics-backend.service; enabled)
   Active: active (running) since Mon 2026-09-15 08:00:00 UTC; 1h 15min ago
 Main PID: 2104 (java)

[admin@srv-analytics ~]$ sudo ss -tulpn
Netid  State   Recv-Q  Send-Q   Local Address:Port   Peer Address:Port  Process
tcp    LISTEN  0       128          127.0.0.1:8080        0.0.0.0:*      users:(("java",pid=2104,fd=14))
tcp    LISTEN  0       128            0.0.0.0:22          0.0.0.0:*      users:(("sshd",pid=842,fd=3))

options.text: Notice the application is listening strictly on loopback (127.0.0.1:8080) rather than all interfaces (0.0.0.0:8080), explaining why external connections are refused.
options.feedback: Optimal: A socket bound to 127.0.0.1 only accepts traffic originating locally within the same OS. External packets arriving on interface 10.20.4.50 are dropped or rejected with TCP RST (Connection refused).

options.text: Disable firewalld on Rocky Linux to see if packets start passing.
options.feedback: Even if firewalld permitted port 8080, the Linux kernel TCP stack rejects external packets addressed to 10.20.4.50 when no listener exists on that IP.

decisionPoints.title: Review Application Configuration and Firewall Rules
decisionPoints.description: Inspect /etc/analytics/application.properties and check firewalld port allowances.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Configuration & Firewall Audit:
[admin@srv-analytics ~]$ cat /etc/analytics/application.properties
server.port=8080
server.address=127.0.0.1
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://db.corp.local:5432/analytics

[admin@srv-analytics ~]$ sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
public (active)
  target: default
  interfaces: eth0
  services: ssh
  ports: 8080/tcp

options.text: Change server.address to 0.0.0.0 in application.properties, restart analytics-backend, and verify remote connectivity.
options.feedback: Optimal: Binding to 0.0.0.0 permits the Java daemon to listen on all IPv4 interfaces, including 10.20.4.50, allowing the firewalld rule (which already allows 8080/tcp) to accept remote client traffic.

options.text: Configure an iptables PREROUTING port forwarding rule to redirect eth0 traffic to 127.0.0.1:8080.
options.feedback: NAT port forwarding to loopback is an unnecessarily complex anti-pattern that obscures client source IPs and adds routing overhead.

finalDiagnosis.title: Application Daemon Bound to Loopback (127.0.0.1) Instead of Network Interface
finalDiagnosis.rootCause: In the recently deployed configuration file (/etc/analytics/application.properties), 'server.address' was set to '127.0.0.1' (default development setting). Consequently, the Java backend daemon only opened a TCP listener on the loopback interface. When remote systems sent SYN packets to the VM's physical IP (10.20.4.50:8080), the Linux network stack replied with TCP RST ('Connection refused') because no application had bound to that network address.
finalDiagnosis.evidenceSummary:
1. VM ping and SSH (port 22) responded normally over the network.
2. 'systemctl status analytics-backend' proved the daemon was running.
3. 'ss -tulpn' revealed local address was '127.0.0.1:8080', not '0.0.0.0:8080'.
4. Configuration file had explicit setting 'server.address=127.0.0.1'.
5. 'firewall-cmd' already had port 8080/tcp allowed.
finalDiagnosis.recommendedRemediation:
1. Edit /etc/analytics/application.properties and configure 'server.address=0.0.0.0'.
2. Restart the application daemon: 'sudo systemctl restart analytics-backend'.
3. Verify socket listener with 'ss -tulpn | grep 8080'.
finalDiagnosis.verificationSteps:
1. From the local server, run 'curl -I http://10.20.4.50:8080/health'.
2. From a remote client on the subnet, test TCP reachability: 'curl -I http://10.20.4.50:8080/health' (HTTP 200 OK).
3. Confirm load balancer backend health checks return healthy.
finalDiagnosis.preventionMeasures: Implement configuration linting in CI/CD deployment pipelines to detect and reject localhost or 127.0.0.1 bindings on production environment profiles.

title: Multiple Failed Authentication Alerts Followed by Sudden Interactive Login
symptoms: SIEM security alert fires: User account 'jdoe' generated 35 failed logon attempts within 3 minutes from an anomalous foreign IP address, immediately followed by a successful interactive authentication and MFA approval.
environment: Enterprise Identity Provider (IdP), Azure AD / Entra ID, Microsoft Defender for Identity, SIEM / SOC Telemetry.
scenarioDescription: As a SOC Tier 2 Security Analyst, an alert flashes on your console: 'Potential Password Spray Succeeded with Push Fatigue Approval'. The user 'jdoe' is an IT Helpdesk Operator holding elevated administrative roles. You must analyze the evidence, assess risk, and execute rapid containment without executing offensive actions.

decisionPoints.title: Triage SIEM Authentication Logs and Geo-Telemetry
decisionPoints.description: Examine the SIEM authentication logs to assess the source IP, user agent, authentication protocol, and target account.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - SIEM Event Log Aggregation:
Timestamp: 2026-09-15T09:40:12Z | User: jdoe@corp.com | EventID: 4625 (Logon Failure) | SourceIP: 185.220.101.42 (Tor Exit Node, NL) | FailureReason: Bad Password | Count: 35 attempts
Timestamp: 2026-09-15T09:43:05Z | User: jdoe@corp.com | EventID: 4624 (Logon Success) | SourceIP: 185.220.101.42 (Tor Exit Node, NL) | AuthType: Password | MFA: Challenged
Timestamp: 2026-09-15T09:43:58Z | User: jdoe@corp.com | EventID: 50074 (MFA Prompt) | Method: Mobile Push Notification | Result: Approved

User Profile: Jane Doe (Helpdesk Operations, Member of: 'Helpdesk-Admins', 'Workstation-Tier1-Operators'). Usual Location: Boston, MA, USA (Workstation IP 73.12.98.22).

options.text: Dismiss the alert as a false positive because the final authentication returned successful with MFA approval.
options.feedback: Never dismiss sudden foreign Tor exit node logins following rapid failed authentication attempts as false positives; this is the classic signature of password spraying followed by MFA push bombing fatigue.

options.text: Examine MFA challenge logs and active sessions to determine if the user intentionally approved the request.
options.feedback: Optimal: Correlating multiple rapid MFA push notifications before approval clarifies whether this was legitimate or an MFA fatigue attack.

decisionPoints.title: Analyze MFA Audit Logs and User Communications
decisionPoints.description: Inspect the Identity Provider's MFA challenge history and contact the user via out-of-band communication (work phone).
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - IdP MFA Challenge Telemetry:
09:43:10Z - Push sent to iPhone 14 - Result: Denied (User report: Not Me)
09:43:22Z - Push sent to iPhone 14 - Result: Denied
09:43:35Z - Push sent to iPhone 14 - Result: Denied
09:43:48Z - Push sent to iPhone 14 - Result: Denied
09:43:58Z - Push sent to iPhone 14 - Result: Approved

Analyst Out-of-Band Phone Interview with Jane Doe:
'My phone started buzzing like crazy with push requests while I was driving to the office. I accidentally tapped Approve just to make the notifications stop!'

options.text: Initiate immediate incident containment: Revoke all active user sessions, reset password, and temporarily disable account.
options.feedback: Optimal: The user confirmed unauthorized push notification spamming and accidental approval. Active sessions established from the adversary IP must be terminated immediately to prevent lateral movement.

options.text: Wait for the user to arrive at work in 30 minutes to review her laptop in person before taking action.
options.feedback: Delaying containment gives the attacker holding an active administrative session 30 minutes to harvest credentials, access directory objects, or create persistence.

decisionPoints.title: Execute Containment and Post-Incident Security Controls
decisionPoints.description: Revoke refresh tokens, assess if any permissions were modified during the 5-minute unauthorized session, and enforce number matching.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - Containment Execution & Audit:
PS C:\> Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken -ObjectId jdoe@corp.com
Success: All OAuth refresh tokens and active sessions revoked.

PS C:\> Set-AzureADUser -ObjectId jdoe@corp.com -AccountEnabled $false
Success: Account temporarily disabled pending credential rotation.

PS C:\> Get-AzureADAuditDirectoryLogs -Filter "initiatedBy/user/userPrincipalName eq 'jdoe@corp.com'" | Select-Object TimeGenerated, ActivityDisplayName
(0 records found during session window - no persistence established).

options.text: Conclude incident containment, rotate credentials with strong password, and upgrade tenant MFA policy to mandatory Number Matching and FIDO2.
options.feedback: Optimal: Account is secured, zero persistence was established, and implementing MFA number matching permanently eliminates blind push fatigue vulnerabilities.

options.text: Attempt to scan and hack back the adversary's Netherlands IP address.
options.feedback: 'Hacking back' is illegal, unethical, and futile against Tor exit nodes. Enterprise defense must focus on identity hardening and containment.

finalDiagnosis.title: Compromised Password via Spraying Exploited Through MFA Push Fatigue
finalDiagnosis.rootCause: An external attacker identified a weak or leaked password for 'jdoe@corp.com' during automated password spraying from Tor exit nodes. When confronted with MFA, the attacker repeatedly triggered 5 push notifications within 50 seconds (MFA fatigue attack). The legitimate user, while distracted, tapped 'Approve' to silence the spam, granting the adversary an active authenticated session.
finalDiagnosis.evidenceSummary:
1. SIEM registered 35 rapid Event ID 4625 failures from Tor IP 185.220.101.42.
2. Successful login occurred from Netherlands IP while user was physically in Boston.
3. IdP MFA logs showed 4 rapid denied prompts followed by a single approved prompt.
4. User confirmed over out-of-band phone call that she accidentally approved the notification to stop phone buzzing.
5. Active session was revoked before directory objects or permissions could be altered.
finalDiagnosis.recommendedRemediation:
1. Revoke all active session tokens and refresh tokens immediately using identity provider PowerShell cmdlets.
2. Temporarily disable the account, conduct an audit of recent directory actions, and reset user password with a high-entropy secret.
3. Re-enable account only after user enrollment in phishing-resistant MFA.
finalDiagnosis.verificationSteps:
1. Verify user cannot sign in with old password or previous session cookies.
2. Review unified audit logs across the tenant during the 5-minute session window to confirm no OAuth apps were consented or mail forwarding rules added.
3. Verify successful re-authentication only occurs after new MFA enrollment.
finalDiagnosis.preventionMeasures: Mandate MFA Number Matching in Microsoft Authenticator or transition to FIDO2 / WebAuthn hardware security keys, which are mathematically immune to push fatigue and adversary-in-the-middle phishing attacks.

title: AWS VPC Web Tier Unreachable Due to Network ACL Return-Traffic Rules
symptoms: EC2 instances hosting an HTTPS web application inside a public AWS VPC subnet can perform outbound HTTP/HTTPS curl commands normally, but external Internet users experience connection timeouts when attempting to connect to https://<Public_IP>, despite the instance Security Group permitting inbound TCP port 443.
environment: Amazon Web Services (AWS) VPC with an attached Internet Gateway (IGW); Public Subnet (10.0.1.0/24) associated with a custom Network ACL (acl-01a2b3c4d5e6f7g8); EC2 Web Server instance running Amazon Linux 2023 with Elastic IP assigned. Architectural Context: Unlike Azure Network Security Groups (NSGs) or AWS Security Groups which operate as stateful firewalls, AWS Network ACLs operate strictly at subnet boundaries as stateless packet filters.
scenarioDescription: A DevOps team deployed a production web service on Amazon EC2 in an AWS VPC public subnet. Security Groups were configured to allow inbound HTTPS (port 443) and all outbound egress. Outbound patch downloads and external API queries succeed from inside the instance, and nginx is confirmed listening on port 443. Yet, all inbound web requests from external clients time out. You must methodically trace the AWS VPC network boundary filters, recognize the stateless nature of AWS Network ACLs, and restore client return traffic.

decisionPoints.title: Verify In-Guest Listener and Security Group Ingress Rules
decisionPoints.description: Log into the EC2 instance via AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Session Manager to verify nginx service health, local socket listeners, and instance Security Group ingress rules.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - In-Guest Web Service & AWS Security Group Inspection:
$ sudo systemctl status nginx
● nginx.service - The nginx HTTP and reverse proxy server
   Active: active (running) since Mon 2026-09-15 10:00:12 UTC; 30min ago

$ sudo ss -tulpn | grep 443
tcp   LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:443  0.0.0.0:*  users:(("nginx",pid=3410,fd=7))

$ aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8
Security Group: web-tier-sg (sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8)
[Inbound Rules]
- Protocol: TCP | Port: 443 | Source: 0.0.0.0/0 (HTTPS Ingress Allowed)
- Protocol: TCP | Port: 22  | Source: 203.0.113.50/32 (Admin SSH Allowed)
[Outbound Rules]
- Protocol: ALL | Ports: ALL | Destination: 0.0.0.0/0 (All Outbound Egress Allowed)

options.text: Reboot the EC2 instance to force an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) reset.
options.feedback: Rebooting the EC2 instance will not solve packet drops caused by network filtering rules. The in-guest socket listener is already healthy and listening on 0.0.0.0:443.

options.text: Confirm that the stateful Security Group is permitting inbound 443, and advance to inspect the subnet-level boundary filter (AWS Network ACL).
options.feedback: Optimal: Because AWS Security Groups are stateful firewalls operating at the virtual network interface layer and clearly permit inbound 443, the connection drop must be occurring at the subnet boundary controlled by AWS Network ACLs.

decisionPoints.title: Audit AWS VPC Subnet Association and Network ACL Inbound Rules
decisionPoints.description: Inspect the subnet association and query the custom Network ACL (NACL) rules applied to the web tier subnet.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - AWS Network ACL Rule Table (aws ec2 describe-network-acls):
NACL ID: acl-01a2b3c4d5e6f7g8 (Associated Subnet: subnet-0123456789abcdef0 [10.0.1.0/24])

[Inbound (Ingress) Entries]
Rule #   Protocol   Port Range   CIDR Block    Action
-----------------------------------------------------
100      TCP        443          0.0.0.0/0     ALLOW
110      TCP        80           0.0.0.0/0     ALLOW
*        ALL        ALL          0.0.0.0/0     DENY (Default)

[Outbound (Egress) Entries]
Rule #   Protocol   Port Range   CIDR Block    Action
-----------------------------------------------------
100      TCP        443          0.0.0.0/0     ALLOW
110      TCP        80           0.0.0.0/0     ALLOW
*        ALL        ALL          0.0.0.0/0     DENY (Default)

options.text: Conclude that because Inbound Rule 100 permits TCP port 443, the Network ACL is correctly configured for external web traffic.
options.feedback: Incorrect assumption: Unlike stateful firewalls (such as AWS Security Groups or Azure NSGs), AWS Network ACLs are completely stateless. An inbound allow rule permits the client SYN packet to enter the subnet, but return packets (SYN-ACK) cannot exit without an explicit outbound rule matching the client's destination port.

options.text: Recognize that AWS Network ACLs are stateless, meaning response traffic requires outbound rules matching the client's ephemeral port range.
options.feedback: Optimal: When a client initiates an HTTPS request to port 443, the client operating system allocates a temporary high-order ephemeral port (typically 1024-65535 or 32768-60999). The server's return packets have destination ports in that ephemeral range, not port 443.

decisionPoints.title: Analyze Ephemeral Port Return Flow and Determine Remediating Rule
decisionPoints.description: Correlate client-server TCP session mechanics with the stateless outbound NACL rule table to formulate the precise egress permission.
decisionPoints.evidence:
Lab Evidence - VPC Flow Logs Telemetry & Packet Tracing:
2 123456789012 eni-01234567 198.51.100.25 10.0.1.50 51432 443 6 1 60 1726398012 1726398072 ACCEPT OK (Inbound SYN allowed by NACL Rule 100)
2 123456789012 eni-01234567 10.0.1.50 198.51.100.25 443 51432 6 1 60 1726398012 1726398072 REJECT OK (Outbound SYN-ACK dropped by NACL default rule *)

Analysis: Inbound client session source port is 51432 (ephemeral port). The server's return packet has source port 443 and destination port 51432. Outbound NACL rule table only allows destination ports 80 and 443; packets destined for port 51432 hit the default DENY rule (*). (Note: In Microsoft Azure, Network Security Groups are stateful and track return traffic automatically; this stateless drop is specific to AWS VPC Network ACLs).

options.text: Add a stateless outbound Network ACL rule allowing TCP ports 1024-65535 to destination 0.0.0.0/0 to permit return traffic to client ephemeral ports.
options.feedback: Optimal: Adding an outbound rule for TCP 1024-65535 allows the web server to send response packets back to any external client's allocated ephemeral port, satisfying the stateless requirement of AWS Network ACLs.

options.text: Reconfigure the web server nginx daemon to send return packets exclusively on source and destination port 443.
options.feedback: TCP sockets cannot override the client's allocated ephemeral source port. In standard TCP/IP networking, the server MUST send return packets to the client's chosen ephemeral port.

finalDiagnosis.title: AWS VPC Web Tier Unreachable Due to Network ACL Return-Traffic Rules
finalDiagnosis.rootCause: AWS VPC Network ACLs operate at subnet boundaries and are strictly stateless packet filters. Although the custom inbound Network ACL allowed TCP port 443 and the instance Security Group was open, the custom outbound Network ACL only allowed destination ports 80 and 443. External web clients initiate connections using client-side ephemeral ports (e.g. 1024-65535). Because AWS Network ACLs do not track connection state (unlike stateful AWS Security Groups or Azure Network Security Groups), the server's return response packets (SYN-ACK / TLS ServerHello) destined for client ephemeral ports were dropped by the subnet outbound default DENY rule (*).
finalDiagnosis.evidenceSummary:
1. In-guest nginx service was running and listening on 0.0.0.0:443.
2. EC2 Security Group permitted inbound TCP 443 and all outbound traffic (-1).
3. Inbound Network ACL Rule 100 allowed TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0.
4. Outbound Network ACL rule table lacked an allow rule for ephemeral ports, permitting only destination ports 80 and 443.
5. VPC Flow Logs proved inbound SYN packets were ACCEPTED, but corresponding outbound return packets to client port 51432 were REJECTED by the subnet NACL boundary.
finalDiagnosis.recommendedRemediation:
1. Add an outbound allow rule to the custom Network ACL: 'aws ec2 create-network-acl-entry --network-acl-id acl-01a2b3c4d5e6f7g8 --rule-number 120 --protocol tcp --port-range From=1024,To=65535 --egress --cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --rule-action allow'.
2. For public web subnets in AWS VPCs, standard architecture requires permitting outbound ephemeral ports (TCP 1024-65535) to 0.0.0.0/0 to support diverse client operating systems (Windows uses 49152-65535, Linux uses 32768-60999, others use 1024-65535).
3. In scenarios where stateless packet filtering at the subnet layer is not explicitly required for compliance or IP-range blacklisting, associate the subnet with the default AWS VPC Network ACL (which allows all inbound/outbound) and rely on stateful Security Groups for granular micro-segmentation.
finalDiagnosis.verificationSteps:
1. Execute 'curl -Iv https://<Public_IP>' from an external client and verify full TCP three-way handshake and TLS session establishment.
2. Query VPC Flow Logs to verify outbound return packets transitioning from REJECT to ACCEPT.
3. Verify external browsers load the web application with HTTP 200 OK.
finalDiagnosis.preventionMeasures: Clearly document cloud security boundary models in team architecture baselines: AWS Security Groups are stateful and enforce rules at the virtual interface layer, whereas AWS Network ACLs are stateless and enforce rules at the subnet boundary. Distinguish AWS stateless NACLs from Azure NSGs, which are stateful by default. Whenever authoring custom AWS NACLs, always configure reciprocal ephemeral port return rules.
